THE BIG IDEA · CACHE-ASIDE
One request, twice: watch where the data comes from
Animated in the browser view. The pattern is called cache-aside: check the cache, fall back to the database, then fill the cache.
WHY CACHE?
Same request, very different response times
MISS · MongoDB
2,000+
milliseconds
The query runs every time. Our code adds a 2 s delay to act like a heavy query.
HIT · Redis Cloud
~250
milliseconds
Measured in our lab. Most of this is internet travel time to the cloud.
HIT · same machine
~2
milliseconds
In real companies Redis sits next to the server, so a hit is almost instant.
Your numbers will differ by network and region. What matters: MISS is always much slower than HIT.

BACKEND · config/redis.js
Connect to Redis, and survive if it is down
client = createClient({   url: process.env.REDIS_URL,          // ①   socket: {     reconnectStrategy: (retries) =>       Math.min(retries * 500, 5000),   // ②   }, }); client.on('ready', () => { isReady = true; });  // ③ client.on('error', () => { isReady = false; }); client.connect().catch(() => {}); function getRedis() {   return isReady ? client : null;      // ④ }
① The link comes from .env, never typed in code.
② If Redis drops, retry every few seconds, up to 5 s apart.
③ Events flip a flag: is Redis usable right now?
④ Down? Return null. Every route then skips Redis and uses MongoDB: header BYPASS.
BACKEND · server.js
Wire the app together, in the right order
app.use(cors({ exposedHeaders: ['X-Cache'] }));  // ① app.use(express.json()); app.get('/api/health', (req, res) => {       // ②   res.json({ server: 'ok',     redis: getRedis() ? 'connected' : 'not connected' }); }); app.use('/api/products', rateLimiter, productRoutes); // ③ (async () => {   await connectDB();    // must work   // ④   connectRedis();       // optional   app.listen(PORT); })();
① Browsers hide custom headers. Without this, React can’t read HIT or MISS.
② Powers the green Redis: connected dot in the UI.
③ rateLimiter runs first on every product request. Test 4 lives here.
④ Waits for MongoDB, but not for Redis. No cache? Still starts.
BACKEND · routes/products.js · GET /api/products
The heart of the lab: cache-aside in three steps
router.get('/', async (req, res) => {   const redis = getRedis();   // ① Try Redis first   if (redis) {     const cached = await redis.get(LIST_KEY);     if (cached) {       res.set('X-Cache', 'HIT');       return res.json(JSON.parse(cached));     }   }   // ② MISS → ask MongoDB (slow)   await slowQuery();   const products = await Product.find().lean();   if (redis) await redis.set(LIST_KEY,  // ③ save       JSON.stringify(products), { EX: CACHE_TTL });   res.set('X-Cache', redis ? 'MISS' : 'BYPASS');   res.json(products); });
① Look in Redis
Found? Send it back at once. MongoDB is skipped: HIT.
② Ask MongoDB
Not found: run the slow query: MISS.
③ Save for later
Store the answer with EX 60, so the next 60 s are fast.
INSIDE REDIS
Redis stores text, so we convert on the way in and out
JS array
[{ name, price }]
stringify
JSON text
'[{"name":…}]'
SET
Redis key
products:all
Redis Insight Workbench or redis-cli
> TYPE products:all string > TTL products:all (integer) 47 > GET products:all "[{\"_id\":\"6ad1…\",\"name\":\"Samsung…
Key naming pattern
products:all · the list
product:<id> · one item
rate:<ip> · a counter
On a HIT the opposite happens: GET returns the text, and JSON.parse turns it back into an array.
FRONTEND · src/api.js + App.jsx
How the page knows HIT or MISS, and how long it took
export async function request(method, url, body) {   const start = performance.now();           // ①   const res = await fetch(url, { method, … });   const ms = Math.round(performance.now() - start);   return {     data: await res.json(), status: res.status,     cache: res.headers.get('X-Cache') || '-',   // ②     ms,   }; }
// App.jsx · CacheBadge picks the colour const kind = cache === 'HIT' ? 'hit'   : cache === 'MISS' ? 'miss' : 'none';     // ③
① Timer starts before the request and stops after the reply.
② Reads the header the backend set.
③ Badge values you will see:
HIT · from Redis
MISS · from MongoDB
BYPASS · Redis down
NONE · not cached yet
- · no header (POST, 429)

TEST CASE 1 · WHAT TTL DOES
A cached key counts down, then disappears by itself
Shown 10× faster than real time. TTL -2 means “no such key”; -1 would mean “key with no expiry”.

TEST CASE 2 · WHAT YOU CHANGE · routes/products.js
After every write, delete the old cached list
// POST /api/products   const product = await Product.create({ name, price, category, description }); + const redis = getRedis(); + if (redis) await redis.del(LIST_KEY);        // throw away the stale list   res.status(201).json(product); // DELETE /api/products/:id   const deleted = await Product.findByIdAndDelete(id);   if (!deleted) return res.status(404).json({ message: 'Product not found' }); + const redis = getRedis(); + if (redis) await redis.del([LIST_KEY, `product:${id}`]);  // list + item   res.json({ message: 'Deleted', id });
Only 4 new lines. Green lines starting with + are the ones you add.
Why DEL, not SET? The next GET rebuilds the list from MongoDB, so it is always correct.

TEST CASE 4 · STOP THE SPAMMER · BEFORE
Anyone can call the API as often as they like
1
Don’t click anything for 60 s
2
Click Send 6 quick requests
3
All six rows say 200
4
KEYS rate:* → (empty array)
The rule you will build
At most 5 requests per minute from one IP address
1 ✓
2 ✓
3 ✓
4 ✓
5 ✓
6 · 429
429 means Too Many Requests. After 60 s the counter resets.
Redis is perfect for this: one shared counter per IP that expires by itself.
Starter rateLimiter.js only calls next(), so every request passes.
TEST CASE 4 · WHAT YOU CHANGE · middleware/rateLimiter.js
Count requests per IP with INCR and EXPIRE
async function rateLimiter(req, res, next) {   const redis = getRedis();   if (!redis) return next();              // ④   const key = `rate:${req.ip}`;   const count = await redis.incr(key);      // ①   if (count === 1)     await redis.expire(key, 60);          // ②   if (count > 5) {                       // ③     return res.status(429).json({       message: 'Too many requests, try again in a minute',     });   }   next(); }
① INCR adds 1 and returns the new count. A missing key starts at 1.
② Start the 60 s window only on the first request, so it can’t keep sliding.
③ Over 5? Stop here with 429. The route never runs.
④ Redis down? Let users through rather than block everyone.

CODING WITH AI, THE RIGHT WAY
AI can write the change. You must understand it.
1
Reproduce the problem with the test case first
2
Give context: file, route, key name, goal
3
Read every line it returns. Does it match the pattern?
4
Re-run the test and match the AFTER slide
5
Explain it in your own words in the viva
A GOOD PROMPT
“In backend/routes/products.js, GET / caches the list in Redis under products:all for 60 s, using getRedis(). After POST the list is stale. Change only the POST route so it deletes products:all after saving. Explain each line you add.”
Never paste your .env, passwords or connection strings into any AI tool.

For one key (products:all) with TTL 60 s. Each write adds one extra read, because DEL forces a refill.
TWO FORMULAS
DB reads ≈ keys × (60 ÷ TTL) + writes
Hit ratio = HITs ÷ requests
At 600 requests: 599 ÷ 600 = 99.8%
Traffic grows 1,000×, MongoDB load stays the same.
Assumes the requests arrive within one TTL window and nothing is written in that minute.
PART 4 · WHERE THE TIME GOES
A HIT skips the slowest parts of the trip
MISS ≈ 2,500 ms
GET
MongoDB query (2,000 ms simulated + network)
SET
HIT ≈ 250 ms
GET
Memory, not disk
Redis keeps data in RAM. No disk reads at all.
Lookup, not query
GET by key is one direct lookup. No query planning or scanning.
Fewer round trips
HIT: 1 trip to Redis. MISS: Redis, MongoDB, Redis again.
Approximate split of our lab run. Our ~250 ms HIT is mostly internet distance; Redis next to the server answers in about 1 ms.
PART 4 · USE IT WISELY
Cache data that is read often and changes rarely
Good to cache
  • Product lists and categories
  • Results of heavy queries or reports
  • Public profile pages
  • Counters like rate limits
Be careful or skip
  • Values that must be exact now: balances, stock at checkout
  • One user’s private data under a shared key
  • Passwords and secrets
  • Data that is already cheap to read
Short TTL fresher data, more DB reads
CACHE_TTL
Long TTL fewer DB reads, older data
VIVA
Eight questions to check understanding
1 What happens to the app if Redis goes down?
2 Why is MongoDB still the source of truth?
3 What does TTL -2 mean? What about -1?
4 Why didn’t the new product appear in Test case 2?
5 Why DEL the key instead of saving the new list?
6 Why does EXPIRE run only when the count is 1?
7 Why was our HIT about 250 ms and not 1 ms?
8 Why is KEYS avoided in production?
Model answers are in the speaker notes.
KEY TAKEAWAYS
Five things to remember from today
1
Cache-aside: check Redis, fall back to MongoDB, then fill Redis.
2
Invalidate on write: DEL the key whenever the data changes.
3
TTL is the safety net: stale data can never live longer than it.
4
Redis is more than a cache: INCR + EXPIRE makes a rate limiter.
5
Measure it: 600 requests, 1 database read. That is the I/O saved.
Extension ideas: sliding-window rate limiter (sorted sets) · sessions in Redis · a live leaderboard with ZADD
